title: AI Basics — Your First Conversation
description: Start from zero: choose an assistant, work through a problem in conversation, build prompts and set up useful context.
useful_result: Independently steer a guided conversation to a useful checked result, then reuse the approach on another task.

pages.title: 01 — What AI Can Do for You
pages.body:
BLI means Big Lever Institute. Our lessons help you use AI as a collaborator while keeping your judgment.

You do not need an AI account, coding experience or special vocabulary to begin. This course takes you from choosing an assistant to getting and improving a useful result. If you already have an account, start at lesson 03. If you already use chats comfortably, choose the later skill you need.

A simple route through this course

Begin with lessons 01–03: understand the tool, open one assistant and make a useful draft. Lessons 04–05 help you ask clearly and work through an unfinished problem. Use 06–08 when you need files, saved instructions or continuing work; those features are optional. Lesson 09 helps you check, keep and use what you made. You can return for a skill when you need it.

A conversation, not a search box

An AI assistant is software you can talk or write to. It can help draft a message, explain a difficult passage, organize notes, compare options or suggest steps. You can reply: “That is too formal,” “Use my notes,” or “Explain that part.” The back-and-forth is part of the work.

It generates answers from learned patterns and the information/tools available to it. A confident, polished answer can still be wrong. It may invent a date, source or fact. You supply the real situation and decide what to use; later lessons show how to check.

Bring the problem; work it through together

You do not have to know the answer, the right method or the perfect prompt before you start. Describe what you are trying to do and where you are stuck. Ask the assistant to help you work through it: ask questions, explain unfamiliar ideas, compare options and suggest a next step. Reply with what fits and what does not. You can ask it to slow down, try another approach or help you describe the problem itself.

This is useful for many kinds of work: writing, learning, planning, building and making decisions. It does not guarantee a solution or make the assistant an authority on every subject. Check consequential facts and actions with appropriate evidence. The skill is steering a useful conversation while keeping your judgment.

Four different things

  • Company: the organization providing the service, such as OpenAI, Anthropic or Google.
  • Assistant/app: the service you open, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
  • Model: the underlying AI producing responses. An app may offer several; you do not need to choose the most advanced one to begin.
  • Plan/subscription: your account's access and usage allowance. Paying may change limits or tools; it does not make every answer correct.

Choose one small useful job

Think of a message you need to write or a short passage you want explained. No task in mind? We will use a fictional neighborhood cleanup invitation. You will not send it or need to reveal personal details.

Next: lesson 02, Choose an Assistant and Open a Chat. You do not need to understand every AI feature before trying one useful conversation.

pages.title: 02 — Choose an Assistant and Open a Chat
pages.body:
Your result here is an open conversation where you can type and receive a reply. Choose one service, not all three. An existing account is fine.

Choose a starting service

  • ChatGPT, by OpenAI: open the official ChatGPT website. Choose sign-in or account creation and follow the offered email or existing-account sign-in route.
  • Claude, by Anthropic: open the official Claude website. Use its offered Google or email route and complete verification.
  • Gemini, by Google: open the official Gemini website. Sign in with a Google account; create one through Google's account screen if needed.

These are starting options, not a ranking or a requirement to use a particular provider. Availability depends on your region, age and account. Work or school accounts can have restrictions.

Start without buying an upgrade

  1. Open the official service link above in another browser tab. Keep this lesson open.
  2. If you already have an account, sign in. Otherwise follow the service's account-creation steps. You handle your own password, verification and terms; BLI does not need them.
  3. Choose the free route if offered. A trial or paid upgrade is optional. If the screen requires a purchase, stop and check the official plan information or try another supported service.
  4. After sign-in, find the message box. If you are in an old conversation, use the new-chat control: ChatGPT uses New chat; Claude has a new-chat button; Gemini uses New chat in its sidebar. The sidebar may need opening on a small screen.

Our classes are always free. An AI company's subscription is a separate purchase. If you later need higher limits or a specific tool, open that service's account/settings area, compare its current plans, billing period, price and renewal terms, and upgrade only if you want to. You can continue these basic text activities without that purchase. If a limit interrupts you, keep your draft locally and return when access resets or use another suitable assistant.

Your AI conversation happens on the assistant’s website, not in a Skool comment or search box. Keep both tabs open. After sending a message there, return to this Skool tab for the next instruction.

Find the basic controls

The message box is where you type. The send/submit button, often an arrow, sends it. A reply is the assistant's answer. A chat is the conversation containing your messages and replies. When lesson 03 gives you a message, click in this box, type or paste that message, then click send. You do not need to upload a file or configure a Project yet.

Next: lesson 03. If account setup blocks you, keep the exact non-private error message for optional community help. Never post a password, verification code or payment details.

Web directions checked October 13, 2026; controls and plans can change. Use the official service's help if a label differs.

pages.title: 03 — Get Your First Useful Result
pages.body:
Use the open chat from lesson 02, or open your chosen assistant and start a new chat. We will turn a few facts into a friendly invitation. It is fictional practice; nothing will be sent.

Copy, paste and send

Copy the complete block below, click the assistant's message box, paste it, then click its send button. On a computer, copy/paste is usually Ctrl+C/Ctrl+V, or Command+C/Command+V on a Mac. On a phone, select text and use Copy/Paste. You can also type the message yourself. Do not copy the lesson headings.

Try this message — no fields to replace

Copy this prompt

Write a short, friendly invitation for neighbors to a fictional park cleanup. The facts are: Saturday, 10 a.m., meeting at the park entrance. Ask people to bring gloves. Do not add a park name, end time or promises I did not provide. Give me the invitation only; do not send it.

The block is a starting example, not the only way to talk to AI. You can begin in your own words: “I need to invite neighbors to a cleanup, but I am not sure what to say. Help me work it out.” If it asks a question, answer it; if you are unsure, say so. Ask it to explain or offer options you can choose between.

Read it before using it

Does it include Saturday, 10 a.m., the park entrance and gloves? Did it invent an end time or a park name? Do not assume the assistant followed every instruction.

Ask it to check — same chat

Copy this prompt

Check that invitation against only the facts I gave you. Point out missing facts or details you added without support. If there is no important issue, say so. Do not rewrite it yet.

Check the critique yourself against the four facts. If nothing important needs changing, keep the draft. You can optionally change its tone to practice a follow-up. Otherwise choose what needs changing. For example, if it added an end time, type: “Remove the end time; I did not provide one.” If the facts are right but it sounds formal, type: “Keep the facts. Make it warmer and keep it to two sentences.” Send your chosen change in the same message box.

Read the revised invitation again. If a fact changed, compare it with the original facts. If it works, copy it into your notes, or leave it in this chat for now. You have asked, checked and decided what to keep or improve.

Your first milestone: you made an invitation, compared it with the supplied facts and chose whether to revise it. That is enough to try a small real task. You do not need a plugin, file upload or Project to continue.

Try your own task: give the facts of a message you need to draft, omitting private details. Keep it unsent until you check it. Next: lesson 04 shows how to make that first request clearer.

pages.title: 04 — Ask for What You Want
pages.body:
A prompt is the message or instructions you give the assistant. It can be a plain sentence. You do not need magic words. A useful request explains the job and gives the information needed to do it.

Give enough to work with

“Write an invitation” leaves the audience, facts and tone open. “Invite my neighbors to Saturday's cleanup at 10 a.m.; ask them to bring gloves; keep it friendly and brief” makes the result easier to judge.

  • Task: what should it help you do?
  • Context: the relevant background and facts.
  • Audience: who will read or use the result?
  • Result: the form, tone and constraints that matter.

Constraints are limits that matter, such as length or facts it must not add. Use only the parts your task needs. For “Explain this word,” one sentence may be enough.

Build a request for your task

Stay in your task's chat, or open a new chat for a different task. Copy the block, replace each bracketed field with your own words, and send it. Delete the brackets after replacing them. Your cleanup invitation from lesson 03 is an easy option.

A simple prompt you can adapt

Copy this prompt

Help me [TASK].

The relevant facts or material are: [FACTS OR TEXT].

This is for [AUDIENCE].

A useful result would be [FORMAT, TONE OR CONSTRAINTS].

If a missing detail matters, ask me. Do not invent facts or take an external action; draft or explain it here.

If it asks a question, answer in the same message box. If you do not know the answer, say so and ask it to leave that detail out or mark it unknown; do not invent an answer.

Check the result — same chat

Copy this prompt

Compare your result with my request and the facts I supplied. What important requirement did you miss, what unsupported detail did you add, or what is unclear for the audience? Identify useful corrections; do not rewrite yet or invent a problem.

Choose a correction and ask for it in your own words. You can say: “Use shorter sentences,” “Explain the second point,” or “Remove that claim because it is not in my notes.” Check changed facts again. If the answer is already useful, keep it.

Carry forward: change the task and facts next time; keep only instructions that helped. Next: lesson 05 helps when you cannot yet describe what you want.

pages.title: 05 — Work Through a Problem with AI
pages.body:
You can ask the assistant to help with the work itself, not just write a prompt. Bring an unfinished problem and use the conversation to find a useful way forward.

Try a guided conversation

Copy this block, replace the one bracketed field with your situation, and send it. If you have a real task, use it. Otherwise use: “I want to organize a fictional neighborhood cleanup, but I do not know where to start.”

Copy this prompt

I am trying to [WHAT I WANT TO DO OR WHERE I AM STUCK]. Help me think it through.

Ask one useful question at a time and wait for my answer. Help me clarify the result I want, the facts we have and what is uncertain. Explain unfamiliar terms with an example. Suggest options and a small next step when there is enough information; let me choose. Do not invent facts or carry out external actions.

Answer in your own words. You can say “I do not know,” “Show me an example,” “What are my options?” or “That suggestion does not fit because…” For the fictional cleanup, use Saturday, 10 a.m., park entrance and gloves if relevant; a park name and end time are unknown.

When a next step seems useful, choose it and ask the assistant to help do that part in the chat. For example: “Let us start with an invitation. Draft it using only those facts.” Read the result, compare facts and request the changes you want. If the conversation circles without helping, ask for a simpler next step or a summary of what is still missing.

Turn the approach into a prompt when useful

You can begin with a rough goal. The assistant can help turn it into a request, but you decide whether its questions and proposed instructions fit.

Start with your unfinished idea

Use a new chat for a different task, or stay in your current chat if you are developing the same task. Copy this block, replace the one bracketed field with what you want help doing, and send it.

Help me describe the task

Copy this prompt

I want help with [MY ROUGH GOAL], but I do not know how to ask for it well.

Help me make a useful prompt. Ask one question at a time about the result I need and any important facts or constraints. Wait for my answer. Once you have enough, draft a short prompt I can review. Put the proposed prompt by itself so I can copy it. Do not invent my situation or claim a long prompt is necessarily better.

No goal in mind? Replace the field with: “writing a fictional neighborhood-cleanup invitation people can act on.” For this example, use these facts if asked: Saturday, 10 a.m., park entrance, bring gloves. No park name or end time is known. Answer each question in the same chat. You can say “I do not know” or “That detail does not matter.” Do not invent facts just to fill an answer.

Choose the instructions, then try them

Read the proposed prompt. Does it describe your goal? Does it add a requirement you did not want? Ask it to remove or change that part. When you accept the prompt, copy only the accepted prompt text, not the surrounding explanation, into a new chat, supply any material it asks for, and send it. A new chat lets you test whether the prompt carries enough context on its own.

Check the prompt using its actual result

Copy this prompt

Review the prompt and the result it produced against what I wanted. Which missing fact, vague instruction or unnecessary demand affected the result? If the prompt worked well enough, say so. Suggest a specific change for my decision; do not rewrite automatically.

In the chat containing your prompt and result, send that check. If your goal is missing from the new chat, start your check message with a sentence describing it. Choose any useful change, revise the prompt and try it again. A polished prompt is only a proposal until you see what it produces.

Next: lesson 06 shows how to supply notes or a file instead of making the assistant guess.

pages.title: 06 — Give AI Text or a File to Work From
pages.body:
Context is information relevant to the current task. A source is material you can inspect, such as your notes or a document. Attaching a file does not guarantee it was read correctly.

First try readable text

Start a new chat. Copy the complete block below and send it. The notes are fictional and safe to use as provided.

Make a checklist from supplied notes

Copy this prompt

Use only these fictional workshop notes to make a short attendee checklist. Do not guess missing facts.

Workshop notes:

Day: Tuesday

Time: 3 p.m.

Place: Room A

Bring: a notebook

End time: not provided

Tell me which details are clear and which important detail would need asking about.

Compare the checklist with the notes. Tuesday, 3 p.m., Room A and a notebook should survive. The end time is unknown, not a fact to invent.

Try attaching a file, if useful

Use a short document you already have permission to share, with sensitive details removed. If you have none, the pasted-text activity above is enough.

  1. Start a chat. Near the message box, look for the attachment/add control. ChatGPT: + or Add files; Claude: +/attachment menu; Gemini: Add files, then Upload Files.
  2. Choose a file from your device and wait until its name/attachment appears. Avoid connecting your whole Drive or inbox for this practice.
  3. Send: “What is the title or first heading of the attached document? Tell me whether you can read its text. If you cannot, say so.” Compare with the document yourself.
  4. Then ask for one useful thing, such as “Turn the attendee instructions in this document into a checklist. Use only the document and flag missing details.”

If uploads are unavailable, blocked or at a limit, paste a short relevant text excerpt instead. For an image or scanned document, check that names/numbers were read accurately; copying text from the original is a useful alternative when possible. A website link alone is not proof the assistant opened it.

Use the check below in the chat containing the checklist you want to check, whether you used pasted notes or a file.

Check the checklist — same chat

Copy this prompt

Check the checklist against the source text you could read. Point out a missing requirement, an invented detail or uncertainty about reading the source. Do not rewrite yet. Tell me what I should compare with the original.

Choose any needed correction and ask for it. Compare the revised checklist with the original. Keep the source available: a summary can lose details.

Next: lesson 07 separates the facts it should use from instructions about how it should help.

pages.title: 07 — Tell the Assistant How to Help You
pages.body:
Instructions tell the assistant how to work. Context gives it relevant information. “Use short sentences” is an instruction. “The event is Tuesday” is a fact. Both can go in a message, but they do different jobs.

Try an instruction in this chat first

Copy this block into a new chat and send it. There are no fields to replace.

Try a response preference

Copy this prompt

For this conversation, explain unfamiliar words in plain language and give one concrete example. Keep your first answer brief; I can ask for more.

Explain what context means when I am using an AI assistant.

Did the answer explain “context” and give an example? If it used confusing words, reply: “Explain that using the workshop notes from lesson 06: Tuesday, 3 p.m., Room A, bring a notebook.” Choose what helped. A preference is a request, not a guarantee of compliance.

Three scopes

  • Message/chat instructions: apply to this conversation as context permits.
  • Project instructions: help guide work inside that particular workspace.
  • Account-wide custom instructions/preferences: can affect other work too. Use them for stable preferences, not one project's dates or facts.

You can keep using chat instructions; changing your account settings is optional.

Where saved instructions live

Read only the route for the service you chose. If you have no saved workspace yet, keep using the chat instructions for now; lesson 08 walks you through creating that workspace. Account-wide settings are optional and do not have identical names or behavior in every app.

ChatGPT

profile/settings → Personalization → Custom Instructions for broad preferences; a Project's settings for that Project's instructions.

Claude

a Project's Instructions area has a control to edit/save them.

Gemini

for continuing work, use a notebook’s instructions; lesson 08 gives the route. Gems and the newer Skills save reusable task instructions. These are different from a continuing notebook.

If Gemini’s controls differ: Google announced personal-account Gems will be replaced by Skills starting November 2026; account availability differs. Follow the official Gemini transition guide if your controls differ. You can always keep the wording in a note and paste it into a chat.

Before saving, read the scope of the setting. Keep a copy of useful wording so you can remove or replace it later. Do not put private facts into a global preference. If you cannot find the saved-instruction feature, paste your preferred instructions at the start of the relevant chat instead.

Check: start a conversation in the place you configured and ask a simple question. Does it follow the preference? If not, clarify the request or check where you saved it. Do not assume that saving instructions guarantees every answer.

Web directions checked October 14, 2026. See the linked official guides in lesson 08 if controls differ.

Next: lesson 08 combines instructions with source material for work you will return to.

pages.title: 08 — Set Up a Project for Continuing Work
pages.body:
A Project groups continuing work, usually with conversations, source material and instructions. Use one when you return to the same topic; a single invitation does not need one. Saving files, instructions and conversations are different actions. Do not assume every new chat knows what happened in another.

A small workspace you can test

Use these fictional source notes; copy only this block into the source/context area when the route below asks for notes.

Source notes — separate from instructions

Copy this prompt

Workshop notes

Day: Tuesday

Time: 3 p.m.

Place: Room A

Bring: a notebook

End time: not provided

Read only the route for the service you chose. Name your workspace “Workshop practice.” Keep it private; you do not need to share it with BLI.

ChatGPT web

  1. open the sidebar → New project → name it.
  2. Add the notes as pasted text or an available source/file.
  3. Open the Project's ••• menu → Project settings to add the instructions below.
  4. Start your practice chat inside that Project.

Claude web

  1. open Projects → new-project control → name it.
  2. In the Project's Context/knowledge area, use +/Add files → text-content option to paste the notes, or upload a permitted file.
  3. In Instructions, use the edit/set control, paste the instructions and save.
  4. Start the chat from the Project page.
  5. The name alone is not your source context.

Gemini web, if Notebooks is available

  1. sidebar → Notebooks → New notebook; name it and begin a chat.
  2. Use Add sources for the source notes.
  3. To save instructions: All notebooks → open this notebook → More → Notebook settings → instructions → Save.
  4. Gemini Notebook must be connected; review any connection request before deciding.
  5. Rollout and account access vary.
  6. Keep Activity affects saved chats and use of past conversations; do not change privacy settings just to complete this lesson.
  7. Use the pasted-context fallback below if the feature is missing or you prefer it.

If you cannot access one of those features, keep your instructions and notes in your own plain text note. Paste both into a new chat when you resume. It takes an extra step and does not promise automatic memory.

Add the instructions and the facts separately

Copy this block into the workspace's instructions field, or the beginning of your fallback chat. The workshop notes belong in source context, not in these general instructions.

Workspace instructions

Copy this prompt

Help me organize the workshop using the notes I provide. Use plain language. Distinguish a supplied fact from a suggestion. Ask me about missing details that matter. Do not invent dates, locations, commitments or approvals. When I request a draft, make it here; do not send or publish anything.

Challenge important unsupported details and let me choose corrections.

For the fallback chat, paste the source-notes block above after these instructions. For a Project or notebook, add those notes to its source/context area. For a notebook, add the notes as source text using the available source control. If that control cannot accept your notes, use the pasted-context fallback.

Check what it retained

Start a fresh conversation inside the saved workspace and ask: “From the workshop notes you can read, when and where is it, what should attendees bring, and is the end time known?” Do not repeat the answers in that test question.

Compare with your saved source: Tuesday, 3 p.m., Room A, notebook, end time unknown. If it cannot read the notes or adds a time, fix the source placement or ask for a correction and repeat the check. In the pasted-context fallback, supply the notes each time; you are checking whether it can read the notes now, not whether it remembers them later.

At a useful stopping point, save an approved decision or summary explicitly as source text or in your own note. Reopen it later and check it. Do not rely on “remember this” as proof of a saved copy you can reopen.

Web guide check: October 14, 2026. ChatGPT Projects · ChatGPT custom instructions · Claude Projects · Gemini notebooks. Features and names change; use the corresponding official guide rather than guessing another app's controls.

Next: lesson 09 helps you check and keep a result, then choose practical work.

pages.title: 09 — Check Your Work and Choose What Comes Next
pages.body:
The useful result is yours, not the assistant's confidence. You can ask it to critique its work, but you still compare important claims with your notes or other evidence.

You can return to a guided conversation whenever you are stuck: describe the problem, ask for one question or an explanation, consider options and choose a small next step. A reusable prompt is useful when the work repeats; an ordinary conversation is enough to begin something unfamiliar.

Make four concrete checks

  • Purpose: does it do the job you asked for?
  • Facts: are names, times, numbers and claims supported?
  • Fit: does the tone and detail suit the person using it?
  • Action: is this only a draft, or did a tool actually create/save something? Look for the actual file or saved draft before believing that action happened.

For current facts, inspect a reliable current source. For calculations, check the inputs and arithmetic. A citation can be wrong; open it and read the relevant part. For a simple invitation, comparing the supplied facts is enough. You do not need an elaborate review for every sentence.

When an assistant can act

Some assistants can work in connected apps. Say whether you want it to read, draft, or make a change, and identify the intended file or account. Review what a connection allows before enabling it. For a draft, say “make it here; do not send or publish.” If you request an action, reopen the actual saved result and check it. Tool availability differs; ordinary chat practice needs no connection. See official connected-app guidance for a concrete example.

Try a changed case

Open a regular new chat outside your Workshop practice Project or notebook. If your assistant has relevant saved preferences or memory, explicitly say these are the facts for this fictional case. Ask for a fictional workshop invitation using Wednesday, 6 p.m., Room B and “bring a pen.” Give those facts explicitly. Choose your own tone/length. This time, build the request yourself or use lesson 04’s template or lesson 05’s helper. Check that it did not carry Tuesday, Room A or the notebook into the new invitation.

Challenge your result — same chat

Copy this prompt

Check this result against my purpose and the facts I supplied. Identify the important unsupported detail, missing requirement or confusing wording, if any. Explain the correction for my decision. Do not invent flaws or rewrite yet.

Choose a correction, request it, and check any changed facts. If no important issue remains, keep the result. You are ready to try another real task; you do not have to master every feature.

Keep useful work where you can find it

Copy the approved result or prompt into a note/document you control, or deliberately save it in your continuing workspace. Name it for the task. A chat in your history can help you return, but access and retained context can change. Avoid putting private work into the community.

Put the basics to work

Everyday AI — Practical Examples applies this approach to an email or résumé. Exercise Library lets you choose another task. The Project Brain exercise builds a thinking partner around your continuing source materials; it is not required for a single draft.

Optional feedback: tell the community where you got stuck or which instruction helped. Share a redacted example only if you want to. No grade, certificate or private-artifact submission is required.
